groups.label: Build products
groups.blurb: Roles that ship things people use directly.

groups.label: Data & AI
groups.blurb: Roles that turn data into answers, models and products.

groups.label: Run it in production
groups.blurb: Roles that keep systems fast, available and safe.

groups.label: Go deeper
groups.blurb: Depth and foundations rather than a single job title.

roles.name: Frontend Developer
roles.blurb: You build the part people actually touch. Structure and style a page, make it work on a phone and a screen reader, then keep it fast as the app grows.
roles.day: Turning designs into components, arguing about state, and chasing the one bug that only happens on Safari.

roles.name: Backend Developer
roles.blurb: You build what the front end talks to. Data models, APIs, authentication, and the decisions about storage and scale that are expensive to reverse.
roles.day: Designing an endpoint, working out why a query got slow, and deciding what happens when the third-party service is down.

roles.name: Full Stack Developer
roles.blurb: You own a feature end to end — the screen, the endpoint, the table behind it, and the deploy. Breadth over depth, which suits smaller teams and startups.
roles.day: Shipping a whole feature yourself, and switching context more often than anyone else on the team.

roles.name: Mobile Developer
roles.blurb: You build for a device with a battery, a flaky connection and an app store between you and your users. You cannot hotfix a phone the way you hotfix a server.
roles.day: Building screens, handling the connection dropping mid-request, and waiting on store review.

roles.name: Game Developer
roles.blurb: You work to a frame budget. One of the few fields where the constant factor genuinely matters and cache behaviour is a design concern.
roles.day: Tuning a mechanic until it feels right, then finding the sixteen milliseconds you need back.

roles.name: AI / ML Engineer
roles.blurb: You put models into production. Increasingly that means building on top of large models rather than training your own, and being the person who knows why the output changed.
roles.day: Evaluating a model, wiring it into a service, and explaining why last week's prompt no longer works.

roles.name: Data Scientist
roles.blurb: You answer questions the business cannot answer by looking. Statistics and experiment design matter more here than any model, and are what separate the role from an analyst.
roles.day: Designing an experiment, finding the confound, and telling someone senior their idea did not work.

roles.name: Data Analyst
roles.blurb: You turn business questions into answers other people act on. The most approachable way into data work, and the one where communication counts most.
roles.day: Pulling the numbers, working out why two dashboards disagree, and presenting the result.

roles.name: Data Engineer
roles.blurb: You build the pipelines everyone else depends on. Closer to backend engineering than to analysis, with a nightly deadline and a lot of other people's assumptions resting on you.
roles.day: Fixing the job that failed at 03:00, and backfilling a day of data without corrupting yesterday.

roles.name: DevOps Engineer
roles.blurb: You make shipping boring. Pipelines, infrastructure described in code, and the containers everything runs in — so releases stop being events.
roles.day: Cutting deploy time, unbreaking a pipeline, and removing a manual step nobody admits doing.

roles.name: Cloud Engineer
roles.blurb: You design and run what everything else sits on. One provider learned properly, described in code, with the identity and cost decisions that quietly define both the security posture and the bill.
roles.day: Reviewing a Terraform change, tightening a permission, and explaining an invoice.

roles.name: Site Reliability Engineer
roles.blurb: Software engineering applied to operations. The distinction from a sysadmin is that you automate the toil away rather than absorbing it, and you agree in advance how much downtime is acceptable.
roles.day: Writing the automation that ends a recurring page, and running the postmortem when it fires anyway.

roles.name: Security Engineer
roles.blurb: You find the assumption that fails. Mostly not exploitation — mostly noticing, containing, and writing down what happened so it does not happen twice.
roles.day: Reviewing a design for the attack nobody modelled, and triaging whether the alert is real.

roles.name: QA Engineer
roles.blurb: You decide what good enough means and prove it. Automation is software, so a suite nobody can maintain is worse than no suite at all.
roles.day: Exploring a feature for the case nobody specified, and stopping a flaky test being ignored.

roles.name: Software Architect
roles.blurb: You make the decisions other people live with for a decade. Not an entry point — it needs delivery experience, because architecture without it produces diagrams nobody can implement.
roles.day: Writing the decision down, and persuading three teams the trade-off is worth it.

roles.name: Blockchain Developer
roles.blurb: You write code that cannot be patched after deployment, holding assets that cannot be clawed back. Security is not a phase of this job, it is the job.
roles.day: Writing a contract, then trying to break it before someone else does.

roles.name: CS Fundamentals
roles.blurb: Not a job title — the foundation under all of them. Operating systems, networks, databases and theory, in the order a degree teaches them.
roles.day: The material that stays true after the framework you learned this year is gone.

roles.name: DSA & Interview Prep
roles.blurb: The path through data structures and algorithms in the order that works, then the practice and interview rounds that turn it into an offer.
roles.day: Solving by pattern rather than by novelty, and redoing the ones you failed.
